headline: High: shared writable state and broad egress make LangGraph→n8n pair prone to data leakage, prompt injection, and cascading automation errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can write application-defined files and shares state via a checkpointer store; n8n can read/write server filesystem and run workflows with many integrations. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if one agent’s output is later parsed by the other. No MCP/shared clipboard is shown, so this is not high.
conditions: IF LangGraph writes attacker-controlled text into shared state or files that n8n later parses as instructions
IF n8n workflow nodes consume file contents from the shared server filesystem without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces
Disable file-based handoff between the agents
Add provenance tags to all shared artifacts
Require human review before n8n executes content produced by LangGraph

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and filesystem access, and LangGraph explicitly handles model provider API keys while n8n handles per-credential secrets and workflow data. Shared state plus server filesystem access makes accidental exposure of sensitive workflow or graph state plausible in default deployments, though not proven critical without a specific sensitive data class.
conditions: IF either agent stores secrets or sensitive workflow payloads in the shared checkpointer/datastore
IF n8n integrations transmit those payloads to external services
mitigations: Store secrets only in dedicated secret managers
Restrict shared state to non-sensitive metadata
Turn off unnecessary integration nodes
Rotate any credentials used in shared workflows
Audit filesystem permissions on the n8n server

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, write files, and use broad network egress. LangGraph shares state via a checkpointer store, while n8n shares state via datastore and connected systems. Concurrent writes to the same mutable resources can corrupt workflows or overwrite artifacts; the profiles do not show locking, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, datastore, or credential store
IF concurrent executions modify shared files or workflow state without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate writable directories
Add an external lock around shared resources
Serialize writes to the datastore
Disable shell/file writes in one agent for shared jobs
Use per-run namespaces for artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is a low-level orchestration framework that can emit agent outputs, and n8n is a workflow automation system that can act on those outputs through integrations and command nodes. If n8n treats LangGraph output as authoritative, a bad or injected result can cascade into external actions such as API calls or command execution. The profiles show no built-in verification boundary.
conditions: IF n8n workflow steps consume LangGraph output without validation
IF downstream n8n nodes trigger emails, API writes, or Execute Command actions based on that output
mitigations: Insert a validation step before any n8n action node
Require schema checks on LangGraph outputs
Block direct execution of free-form text
Add human approval for destructive workflow steps
Log and diff intermediate outputs before acting

E_compliance.rationale: LangGraph touches graph state defined by the application, while n8n processes whatever workflow data and connected systems provide. Their retention and residency policies are not documented here, so a mismatch is plausible if regulated data flows through both. Because no specific jurisdiction or regulated class is stated, medium is the cautious choice rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through both agents
IF one system retains workflow or graph state longer than the other
mitigations: Classify data before routing it
Set matching retention windows
Avoid sending regulated data to either agent
Document residency for each datastore
Review vendor compliance docs before deployment
